paragraphs: Buffalo Billiards lost to New Orleans Aints 66.8–109.1.
Buffalo lost by more than forty with Terry McLaurin on zero, but the real argument belongs to Ryan Flournoy versus Emanuel Wilson: 20.3 recoverable points sat unused.
Even the corrected lineup would lose. That is not a defense of the choice; it is an indictment of the whole afternoon.

Laiatu Latu (14.6 pts) and Rashan Gary (14.1 pts) were Buffalo's only real reason to keep watching; even together they couldn't supply the offense that Terry McLaurin (0.0 pts) failed to produce. When defenders are carrying the highlights of a forty-two-point loss, congratulating the stars and ignoring the wreck behind them is just a nicer way to avoid the problem.

Emanuel Wilson scored 28.0 while Ryan Flournoy managed 7.7 in the same starting spot — a 20.3-point miss. Even with Emanuel Wilson's extra 20.3, Buffalo Billiards would still lose by 22.0. That FLEX mistake cost real points, but the Aints still had the stronger team. Buffalo needs both a better lineup card and a functioning offense.
The FLEX call deserves explaining. The rest of the defeat deserves a broader investigation, because one correct choice still leaves a brutal margin.
A forty-two-point loss is not a paperwork error. This manager needs to explain why an entire offense vanished while the defensive contributors were left to carry the embarrassment.
Latu earned his praise by making the scoreboard move while too many teammates treated that as optional.
Crowd mood: -22.0 (Sports-Radio Grumbling).

In the Fleeced! cartoon version of Buffalo, the complaint line is jammed and a fellow is sharpening a pitchfork that even his neighbors think is premature. This is grumbling, not a siege; the manager has been granted the courtesy of one more explanation.

A restless -22 rating is a remarkably restrained verdict on this wreck. It says the public is grumbling, not preparing a parade of pitchforks; management should thank its lucky stars that the mood meter hasn't seen fit to use stronger language.

The trust problem is bigger than a single lineup mistake. With a defeat this heavy, supporters need evidence that the manager can distinguish a bad selection from a roster that simply isn't good enough. The next game is an audition for credibility, not merely a chance to improve a decimal.
Next opponent: New England Patriots.
The Patriots will inherit a Buffalo manager who has already been handed a very expensive lesson about FLEX choices. The question is whether he reads it or uses it as a coaster.
Miami Dolphins beat Tampa Bay Buccaneers 134.8–115.8.
Miami scored 134.8 and somehow still left 27.6 points the manager could have gained on the bench by starting Nik Bonitto ahead of Nick Emmanwori.

The manager won. The victory is not a pardon for every decision that preceded it. With Tetairoa McMillan putting up 45.2, there was quite enough help to avoid discovering how much trouble that mistake might have caused.

Tetairoa McMillan (45.2 pts) was so spectacular that Jonathan Taylor's (22.7 pts) excellent afternoon almost became an afterthought. That's a problem the Dolphins would love to have every week. McMillan and Taylor gave Miami a real two-man showcase, the kind of scoring day most managers would frame and hang above the television.
McMillan’s 45.2-point explosion is a Fleeced! breakout worth taking seriously. His score made even a 22.7-point afternoon from Jonathan Taylor feel like the opening act.

Nick Emmanwori scored 30.1 while Nik Bonitto managed 2.5 in the same starting spot — a 27.6-point miss. The win would have grown by 27.6. The manager can enjoy the result and still explain why Nik Bonitto started ahead of Nick Emmanwori.
The bench decision is indefensible even in victory. Winning with this much firepower shouldn't require the manager to audition for Most Fortunate Employee.
Miami can enjoy the offensive fireworks and still give its defensive depth a hard look before the Jets arrive. McMillan cannot be expected to score 45.2 every Sunday.
McMillan earned the applause. The manager can clap along instead of accepting an award for selecting him.
Crowd mood: 13.0 (Cautious Belief).

Miami's imaginary victory parade has one convertible, several suspiciously expensive bottles of champagne and a nervous passenger double-checking the lineup card. The fans are smiling, but nobody has surrendered the right to ask why the coach made winning this difficult.

A cautiously positive 13 after a 134.8-point victory is not ingratitude. It means supporters like what happened without being ready to hand the manager a lifetime contract and the keys to the stadium.

The gap between thrilling talent and full confidence is management's own doing. Fans have every reason to enjoy the fireworks while wondering why a winning team still needed luck to cover a glaring lineup decision. Trust is harder to score than fantasy points.
Next opponent: New York Jets.
The Jets get the glamorous offense next. Miami's challenge is to win without needing its best player to turn every managerial error into a harmless footnote.
New England Patriots lost to Carolina Panthers 106.3–110.2.
Every Patriots starter produced at least 7.4 and the team still lost by 3.9.

There is no mystery bench genius to applaud and no single goat to drag through the town square. Sometimes the opponent gets four more points. A responsible manager will hate that answer because it offers nobody convenient to fire.

Greg Rousseau (25.0 pts) and Drake Maye (24.5 pts) were outstanding, and the rest of New England actually showed up. Losing that kind of game by fewer than four points is agony, but it isn't a license to arrest the lowest scorer for crimes against the standings. The Patriots were competitive from top to bottom; sometimes that earns only a deeply annoying loss.
New England fielded seven contributors and still lost a close one. There is no defensible reason to invent a bench savior just to put somebody on trial.

New England didn't have a bench player who could clearly win this game instead. Sometimes the other side simply plays a little better; inventing a coaching scandal is a poor substitute for looking at a good lineup that lost.
Nobody deserves to be publicly fired for losing a game by four when all the starters contributed.
Rousseau's production kept this competitive. That effort deserves credit even if the result won't cooperate.
Crowd mood: 11.0 (Cautious Belief).

At the fictional Patriots supporters' club, the bartender has poured two drinks: one for the effort and one for the four-point wound. Nobody knows whether to toast or throw the television remote; the team played well enough to make losing particularly offensive.

The near-neutral 11 feels exactly like a fan base trying to decide whether a narrow defeat deserves anger or reluctant applause. Nobody needs a fabricated scapegoat just to make disappointment more satisfying.

Supporters have a functioning team and an infuriating loss. That is a more complicated feeling than fury, even if fury would make for better radio. A sensible fan can keep confidence in the lineup and still spend Monday profoundly irritated.
Next opponent: Buffalo Billiards.
Buffalo comes next, and New England shouldn't let a close loss tempt it into wrecking a lineup that broadly did its job. Losing narrowly is miserable; panic is optional.
New York Jets beat Atlanta Falcons 80.9–51.6.
The Jets beat Atlanta by nearly thirty even though three starters failed to reach five.

Cooper DeJean did not merely lead the team; his 27.5 helped cover an impressive amount of passenger luggage. Management can enjoy the win and still explain how Ollie Gordon outscored the selected Chig Okonkwo by 15.5.

Cooper DeJean (27.5 pts) made Atlanta miserable, and Kirk Cousins (20.5 pts) helped keep the scoreboard respectable. Three Jets starters still failed to crack five points. Winning by nearly thirty with that much dead weight is impressive in the same way crossing a river with three holes in your boat is impressive: enjoy the arrival, then fix the boat.
DeJean's 27.5 is the kind of Fleeced! standout that makes a manager look clever. Three teammates under five are the warning that this act needs more than one headliner.

Ollie Gordon scored 18.0 while Chig Okonkwo managed 2.5 in the same starting spot — a 15.5-point miss. The win would have grown by 15.5. The manager can enjoy the result and still explain why Chig Okonkwo started ahead of Ollie Gordon.
The unused eligible production was an avoidable mistake covered by Atlanta's spectacular generosity. That is not the kind of business model that survives December.
Three starting slots failed to reach five and Atlanta was generous enough not to care. The manager cannot count on the next opponent sharing that charitable disposition.
DeJean should receive the flowers, and perhaps the keys to the building; he carried enough of Sunday's operation already.
Crowd mood: -5.0 (Jury Still Out).

The Jets' pretend victory march has a brass band playing while half the spectators inspect the wheels for missing bolts. Even after a comfortable win, a crowd at minus five isn't rushing to bronze the manager.

A negative five after a comfortable win is a wonderful indictment of the manager's public relations department. The scoreboard says celebrate; the mood meter responds with a suspicious glance at the lineup card.

Jets supporters apparently haven't mistaken rescue for competence. The interesting question is whether management treats this win as vindication or as a warning it got away with something. An ugly victory can buy points in the standings without purchasing a single ounce of trust.
Next opponent: Miami Dolphins.
Miami is unlikely to be nearly as generous as Atlanta. The Jets need a starting group that doesn't require Cooper DeJean to serve as quarterback, running back and fire marshal all at once.
Baltimore Ravens lost to Arizona Cardinals 65.6–94.6.
Brock Bowers scored 20.6, Aaron Rodgers scored 19.2, and four Ravens starters stayed under five.

Those are not little leaks around the edges; that is a roster taking on water with the captain pointing at the excellent lifeboat. The verified Dohnte Meyers alternative would have improved the lineup, but still not rescued a 29-point defeat.

Brock Bowers (20.6 pts) and Aaron Rodgers (19.2 pts) accounted for most of Baltimore's credible offense, while Darnell Mooney (0.0 pts) finished with nothing. Four starters under five is too broad a collapse to pin on one unlucky player. The Ravens had the star attractions and apparently forgot they also needed the rest of the show.
Bowers gave Baltimore a credible scorer. Shame the rest of the lineup couldn't agree on the concept.

Dohnte Meyers scored 15.2 while Darnell Mooney managed 0.0 in the same starting spot — a 15.2-point miss. Even with Dohnte Meyers's extra 15.2, Baltimore Ravens would still lose by 13.8. The spare points mattered, although they would not have bought a victory. The manager cannot sell one substitution as the cure for a roster-wide problem.
One bench correction would have helped, not repaired Baltimore's systemic failure. Management needs to stop presenting a bandage as a structural renovation.
The manager cannot solve four quiet starting positions by talking louder about Brock Bowers.
Crowd mood: 1.0 (Jury Still Out).

Baltimore's imaginary fan meeting has one man demanding pitchforks and six others asking him to wait until the team remembers how to fill its starting spots. The patience is almost more insulting than fury.
A mood of plus one after that showing is almost comically patient. It is the emotional equivalent of reading the damage report, sighing, and deciding to see whether anybody learned anything.

The concern isn't that Baltimore had a bad day; supporters can survive a bad day. It's whether the same unsupported starters will be marched out again while management points admiringly at the few people who did their jobs. Patience is not the same thing as confidence.
Next opponent: Cleveland Browns.
Cleveland is next. Baltimore cannot keep presenting Bowers and Rodgers as an alibi for everybody else; the weak starting slots must become actual contributors.
Cincinnati Bungals lost to Los Angeles Rams 72.9–93.4.
Bijan Robinson provided 27.7, yet Cincinnati lost by 20.6.

Courtland Sutton's 1.4 was ugly, but the documented 15.5-point miss involved Quentin Lake and Boye Mafe. Blame the actual decision, not whichever player happens to be easiest to mock after scrolling to the bottom.

Bijan Robinson (27.7 pts) gave Cincinnati a genuine headliner, and DK Metcalf (16.5 pts) supplied useful help. Courtland Sutton (1.4 pts) left a conspicuous hole in the supporting cast. Robinson deserved a better ending than watching his standout afternoon get buried in a comfortable defeat.
Bijan did his job. A player shouldn't need to score an entire lineup's worth of points to earn a decent result.

Boye Mafe scored 19.0 while Quentin Lake managed 3.5 in the same starting spot — a 15.5-point miss. Even with Boye Mafe's extra 15.5, Cincinnati Bungals would still lose by 5.1. The unused bench production should bother Cincinnati, but the final deficit demands more than a Monday-morning lineup correction.
Boye Mafe's verified advantage is the proper coaching complaint. Courtland Sutton being the lowest scorer doesn't make him automatically the wrong selection.
Cincinnati's stars don't owe the rest of the roster a weekly rescue operation. If the coach thinks one standout makes the other weak spots invisible, the final score respectfully disagrees.
Crowd mood: -5.0 (Jury Still Out).

In the Bengals' fictional town square, frustrated fans arrive with a cart of unused pitchforks, then leave one chair under a spotlight and a sign reading 'EXPLAIN YOUR DEFENSE.' That minus-five reading is the sound of accountability clearing its throat.
Minus five is not outright rebellion. It's the uneasy silence after a loss when supporters know exactly which decision deserves questions and are waiting to hear whether the manager does too.

There is a difference between accepting a superior opponent and accepting an avoidable coaching error. Cincinnati's audience can do the first without offering the second a free pass. The manager would be wise not to confuse restrained frustration with approval.
Next opponent: Pittsburgh Steelers.
Pittsburgh offers another chance to prove that the Bungals' coach knows the difference between having a good player and choosing a good lineup.
Cleveland Browns lost to Seattle Seahawks 53.7–105.0.
Cleveland lost by 51.3. Joe Burrow and Roman Wilson were productive; several others apparently regarded scoring as optional.
Mike Gesicki could have improved the starting card by 10.8, which is worth criticizing, but this defeat needed a rescue operation, not a decorative bench rearrangement.

Joe Burrow (21.8 pts) and Roman Wilson (17.4 pts) delivered respectable totals on a team that lost by more than fifty. Christian Gonzalez (0.0 pts) gave the supporting cast a particularly convincing impression of an empty roster slot. Cleveland's two functioning scorers were playing football; far too much of the rest was apparently submitting an absence request.
Burrow kept the score from looking even more extraordinary. The supporting cast might send a thank-you note.

Mike Gesicki scored 13.0 while AJ Barner managed 2.2 in the same starting spot — a 10.8-point miss. Even with Mike Gesicki's extra 10.8, Cleveland Browns would still lose by 40.5. One better selection would only have changed the size of the bruise. Cleveland needs a larger answer than rearranging the chairs.
The Gesicki alternative was real but not even close to enough. A manager who sells that repair as salvation ought to be handed the final score.
A ten-point bench fix is not an alibi for getting beaten by more than fifty.
Crowd mood: 9.0 (Jury Still Out).

Cleveland's satirical fan club has ordered a marching band for the protest, then postponed it because even the band couldn't agree who should be blamed first. The plus-nine mood is an astonishing courtesy after this beating.
Plus nine after a demolition is a strange kind of mercy, and the mood meter suggests supporters haven't yet turned one embarrassing Sunday into a referendum on everybody's employment.

That restraint shouldn't be mistaken for blindness. A fifty-point beating asks questions about the whole team, not just one lineup slot. If the next response is another motivational speech rather than actual improvement, that thin reserve of goodwill is going to look very expensive.
Next opponent: Baltimore Ravens.
Baltimore is coming off its own shambles. That might sound comforting, until Cleveland remembers it was beaten by fifty-one. One of these managers will have to find a functioning supporting cast.
Pittsburgh Steelers lost to San Francisco 49ers 56.9–90.0.
Pittsburgh started two running backs who scored zero. That is a fairly radical interpretation of the position's purpose.
Rachaad White's 0.0 had an eligible 4.5-point alternative, but the Steelers were buried by 33.1. One modest improvement is not a license to pretend the other problems disappeared.

Robert Spillane (14.0 pts) and Khalil Shakir (13.2 pts) at least gave Pittsburgh a pulse. Meanwhile Rachaad White (0.0 pts) and the other starting running back combined for nothing. Pittsburgh's backfield submitted a zero-point demonstration project. The audience would like its Sunday refunded.
Spillane made an honest contribution to a lineup determined to turn his afternoon into a footnote.

Ted Hurst scored 4.5 while Rachaad White managed 0.0 in the same starting spot — a 4.5-point miss. Even with Ted Hurst's extra 4.5, Pittsburgh Steelers would still lose by 28.6. The bench offered a way to make the result respectable, not a route to victory. Pittsburgh has an entire backfield to explain.
There was a modest available replacement, but the central failure is a backfield incapable of scoring. The coaching discussion shouldn't end with one minor upgrade.
Two zero-point running backs is the roster equivalent of leaving the engine at home and blaming the tires.
Crowd mood: -1.0 (Jury Still Out).

Pittsburgh's imaginary supporters brought pitchforks, then exchanged them for magnifying glasses to locate the missing running-back production. At minus one, fury hasn't arrived; bewilderment already owns the building.
The nearly neutral minus one is a statistical miracle of public patience. Two starting running backs contributed nothing, yet the crowd reading has somehow not fallen through the floorboards.

Supporters can forgive a dreadful afternoon more readily than management pretending it wasn't dreadful. The public mood is hovering near indifference, which should worry a manager almost as much as outrage: at least furious people still expect something.
Next opponent: Cincinnati Bungals.

Cincinnati awaits. Pittsburgh needs its backfield to do something radical: register points. A coaching staff preparing an elaborate speech should first check whether its running backs have actually scored.
Houston Texans lost to Dallas Cowboys 62.2–91.2.
Houston finished with 62.2 while Dallas found 91.2. The nearest thing to a bright spot was Michael Wilson's 16.5, which is a grim standard for celebration.
The Walter Nolen alternative was worth 9.8 more than Terrel Bernard, yet even that would not erase the loss. The criticism belongs in the lineup and the wider roster.
One correction to the lineup does not explain a team beaten by nearly thirty. Houston's bigger problem is how little support its useful scorers received.

Michael Wilson (16.5 pts) and Rome Odunze (15.4 pts) made the game briefly interesting, but DJ Moore's (2.7 pts) tiny contribution helped turn the rest of the roster into a cautionary tale. Houston didn't lose because it lacked any talent. It lost because two useful afternoons were stranded inside a lineup that couldn't offer them meaningful company.

Walter Nolen scored 15.8 while Terrel Bernard managed 6.0 in the same starting spot — a 9.8-point miss. Even with Walter Nolen's extra 9.8, Houston Texans would still lose by 19.2. The reserve outscored the starter, and Houston still had other problems to solve. Two truths can fit in one embarrassing box score.
Walter Nolen was the actual alternative the manager missed. Fixing the slot would make Houston less embarrassing, not turn a twenty-nine-point loss into a moral victory.
Michael Wilson did what he could. His reward was watching the rest of the team fail to create a competitive total.
Crowd mood: -12.0 (Sports-Radio Grumbling).

At the fictional Texans fan rally, the protest signs are still blank because management keeps providing too many candidates for the headline. At minus twelve, the crowd still has patience. Management appears determined to test how quickly that changes.

Houston's fans sit at minus twelve: annoyed, but not yet hopeless. Their team just offered up an afternoon whose main selling point was that a few players remembered football requires scoring. Management should appreciate that the crowd hasn't requested an itemized refund.

The manager should worry less about defending an individual choice and more about whether supporters believe the project has a direction. One corrective substitution won't inspire faith if the entire roster keeps looking like somebody's unfinished draft.
Next opponent: Jacksonville Jags.
Jacksonville is next, and Houston needs a plan extending beyond hoping Michael Wilson can make sixty-two look respectable. Management already has evidence of an avoidable selection problem.
Indianapolis Colts beat New York Giants 107.2–102.6.
Indianapolis survived the Giants by 4.6 thanks in part to Foyesade Oluokun's 32.0.

Every other win this narrow produces a fashionable demand for one player to be blamed. Josh Downs scored 4.6; without a documented legal improvement, calling it a managerial crime is just lazy outrage dressed as analysis.
There is no documented managerial scandal. Calling one into existence after a victory would be the dumbest decision of the weekend.

Foyesade Oluokun (32.0 pts) was the difference-maker Indianapolis needed, and Alvin Kamara (22.8 pts) made sure this wasn't a one-man rescue mission. Josh Downs (4.6 pts) had the quietest afternoon, yet the Colts survived a genuine fight. Criticizing a productive winning lineup as if the manager had committed sabotage would be lazy; winning a game this close is difficult enough without inventing new crimes.
Indianapolis has no demonstrated higher-scoring bench answer here. The critique belongs to the production on the field, not to a substitute nobody can prove would help.
The absence of a proven better lineup is a fact, not permission to invent one. Indianapolis won; treat that as evidence of competent work instead of demanding a villain.
Oluokun was the engine of this win. The rest of the team owes him dinner, not a long explanation of percentages.
Crowd mood: 5.0 (Jury Still Out).

Colts fans in this very imaginary scene pop a modest bottle of champagne, spill half of it during the final-score scare and decide the victory parade can wait until their pulses normalize. Plus five is relief wearing a thin party hat.

Plus five after surviving by fewer than five points is not a victory parade. It's a cautious nod from supporters who watched the finish and would prefer not to require a medical examination afterward.

There is no need to manufacture a managerial crime out of a win. Fans can demand calmer Sundays while admitting the lineup earned this result. Trust built on narrow escapes is fragile, but at least Indianapolis has an actual victory to put underneath it.
Next opponent: Tennessee Titans.
Tennessee won't be required to make the Colts sweat quite so much as the Giants did, but Indianapolis should not confuse a narrow escape with a requirement to dismantle a functioning card.
Jacksonville Jags lost to Washington Commanders 75.6–89.2.
Jacksonville lost by 13.6 with Denzel Ward, RJ Harvey, and Cam Ward holding up most of the operation.

Antoine Winfield offered ten more points than selected Jalen Carter. Ten points is real criticism; pretending it equals thirteen-point-six would require a calculator with very unusual political loyalties.
The manager had more than one issue in a loss this narrow. Spending the whole postgame briefing on one defensive slot would be a convenient way to ignore the surrounding failures.

Denzel Ward (21.0 pts) and RJ Harvey (19.3 pts) gave Jacksonville a credible chance to win; they were doing the heavy lifting while the supporting cast struggled to finish the job. Jalen Carter (3.0 pts) contributed almost nothing, leaving Ward and Harvey to carry a supporting cast that looked far too comfortable watching the highlights. Jacksonville had enough star power to make the loss sting.

Ward's 21.0 and Harvey's 19.3 were Jacksonville's Fleeced! bright spots, but neither could erase the missing production elsewhere. Their manager has explanations to make that have nothing to do with their effort.

Antoine Winfield scored 13.0 while Jalen Carter managed 3.0 in the same starting spot — a 10.0-point miss. Even with Antoine Winfield's extra 10.0, Jacksonville Jags would still lose by 3.6. The manager missed available points, but the Jaguars' defeat was bigger than that one choice. Treating it as a single bad button press would be convenient fiction.
Winfield's advantage was genuine and insufficient. The manager should fix the obvious error without selling it as a machine capable of reversing a thirteen-point-six defeat.
Denzel Ward played well enough to merit a better ending. Sadly, football doesn't award partial credit for deserving.
Crowd mood: 4.0 (Jury Still Out).

Jacksonville's fictional supporters have rolled a ten-point receipt under the manager's door rather than bringing out the pitchforks. They can see the missed defensive call, but they can also see ten points wouldn't cover a 13.6-point defeat.

Plus four for a loss with a real lineup error is a surprisingly generous crowd assessment. The rating says skepticism, not an organized mutiny, and the manager shouldn't mistake that distinction for a compliment.

Supporters have reason to be irritated because the available correction was substantial without being enough to reverse the result. That is the worst kind of accountability conversation: nobody can promise one neat fix, and nobody gets to pretend the obvious mistake was harmless.
Next opponent: Houston Texans.
Houston is next. Jacksonville should revisit its defensive selection without pretending a ten-point repair fixes the rest of its issues. The team lost by more than the spare points could recover.
Tennessee Titans beat Philadelphia Eagles 67.6–53.0.
Tennessee won with 67.6. Yes, that is the full winning score.

Philadelphia was somehow even worse at 53.0, which is the kind of neighborly generosity managers should not expect twice. Deebo Samuel contributed 18.0; the Titans deserve the win, but announcing an offensive revolution after this performance would be deranged.
The manager escaped this one. Please don't confuse escaping with conquering; the offense still has work to do.

Deebo Samuel (18.0 pts) and Juwan Johnson (11.9 pts) were Tennessee's few reliable contributors, and that was somehow enough to win. Philadelphia made the bar so low it could be stepped over without stretching. The Titans are entitled to the victory; declaring this a masterpiece of roster construction would require a very forgiving art critic.

Drue Tranquill scored 19.5 while Carson Schwesinger managed 6.0 in the same starting spot — a 13.5-point miss. The win would have grown by 13.5. The manager can enjoy the result and still explain why Carson Schwesinger started ahead of Drue Tranquill.
Winning with fewer than seventy points should inspire gratitude toward Philadelphia, not an ambitious thesis about coaching brilliance.
Deebo did something useful in a game where usefulness was apparently a scarce commodity.
Crowd mood: 8.0 (Jury Still Out).

Tennessee's imaginary celebration features one party popper, a discount champagne bottle and an announcer urgently asking everyone not to read the final score aloud. Plus eight is approval with its coat already on.
Plus eight after winning with 67.6 is a suitably modest reading. The fans are accepting the win, not requesting a bronze statue of everybody involved.

There's a difference between being pleased your opponent was even worse and believing your own team has found the formula. Supporters would like a victory they can brag about without having to explain the score first. Management has a week to consider that unreasonable luxury.
Next opponent: Indianapolis Colts.
Indianapolis arrives after a game the Titans won largely because Philadelphia couldn't summon sixty points. A sturdier opponent may demand a genuinely respectable offensive score.
Denver Doncos beat Minnesota Vikings 116.3–106.2.
Denver scored 116.3 and needed almost every bit of it against Minnesota's 106.2.

Javonte Williams delivered 31.3 while Andrew Van Ginkel barely appeared on the scoring sheet. That is a victory built with actual production, not a reason to nominate the quietest starter for public execution.

Javonte Williams (31.3 pts) and Nico Collins (30.8 pts) were both devastating, which is why Denver had enough firepower to survive a real Minnesota challenge. Andrew Van Ginkel (1.5 pts) contributed almost nothing, but this wasn't a victory borrowed entirely from the opponent's incompetence. Denver's stars earned it; management's next job is to make sure those stars don't need to file overtime claims every Sunday.
Crowd mood: 17.0 (Cautious Belief).

In Denver's satirical streets, champagne is spraying, a few fireworks are going off and somebody is already sketching an unnecessarily large statue of Javonte Williams. Plus seventeen is real optimism; management's job is to keep the statue from becoming a one-week monument.

Plus seventeen reflects justified optimism without quite becoming an engraved championship invitation. Denver earned its points against serious opposition, so the approval has more substance than the usual victory-induced hysteria.

Supporters should feel encouraged by a team that genuinely had to perform. They should also expect the manager to protect that standard. Confidence isn't an entitlement; it's what happens when the lineup gives people something real to believe in.

Ernest Jones scored 36.3 while Andrew Van Ginkel managed 1.5 in the same starting spot — a 34.8-point miss. The win would have grown by 34.8. The manager can enjoy the result and still explain why Andrew Van Ginkel started ahead of Ernest Jones.
There is no excuse to turn every quiet starter into a firing offense after a real competitive win. The manager's task is to preserve what worked.
The coach deserves an assessment of the full result, not a ceremonial reprimand for whichever player finished last.
Javonte earned an actual winning performance, not just the honor of standing out in a loss.
Next opponent: Los Angeles Chargers.
The next lineup has to survive something more difficult than optimism: an opponent paying attention to Javonte Williams. Denver's depth needs to make the case.
Kansas City Chiefs lost to Green Bay Packers 9.5–27.9. Only Jeffrey Bassa scored for the entire starting lineup.
Jeffrey Bassa supplied every single one of Kansas City's 9.5 points.

Six other starters contributed zero. This is beyond a disappointing supporting cast; it is a group project in which one person did all the work and the others were apparently absent from the classroom. The Chiefs lost 27.9 to Green Bay and still made their opponent's day look respectable.

Jeffrey Bassa (9.5 pts) scored literally every point Kansas City managed. Michael Burton (0.0 pts), Kalen King (0.0 pts), and everyone else supplied zero. There is no meaningful supporting-cast ranking here: first place belongs to Bassa, second place belongs to the concept of participating, and the remaining roster apparently declined its invitation.
Bassa accounted for all 9.5 Kansas City points. That's an unmistakable Fleeced! red flag for the supporting cast: six starters and not a single useful contribution among them.
Crowd mood: -18.0 (Sports-Radio Grumbling).

Kansas City's imaginary fan procession moves toward the front office carrying six cardboard zeros and a handwritten demand for signs of life. The crowd is only at minus eighteen, which is merciful considering almost the whole team forgot how to score.

Kansas City fans registering only minus eighteen after six starters scored zero may be the week's greatest act of charity. The crowd has granted management one more hearing. Six zeroes from the starting lineup will make the defense's opening statement particularly awkward.

At this point supporters aren't demanding sophisticated strategy. They would probably settle for more than one person showing up on the scoresheet. Management has until the next kickoff to offer evidence of a functioning plan. The supporters have already seen enough zeros for one season.
Kansas City's starters supplied almost nothing. Searching the bench for an imaginary single rescuer misses the much uglier story on the field.
Management has to address a lineup-wide shutdown. There is no single benched hero in evidence who turns 9.5 into competitiveness.
The entire lineup after Bassa belongs on the hot seat. An inquiry into just one spot would be suspiciously merciful.
Bassa scored literally everything Kansas City had. Giving the cool throne to anybody else would require a very creative calculator.
Next opponent: Las Vegas Raiders.
Las Vegas somehow offers an opponent with an even emptier scorecard. This is a rare chance for Kansas City to establish whether its seven starting spots are merely ornamental.
Las Vegas Raiders lost to Detroit Lions 0.0–84.0. Every verified starter finished on zero.
Seven starters, seven zeroes, zero points. Las Vegas lost 84.0 to nothing.

There is no clever lineup adjustment that transforms this into a near miss. The manager could have submitted a blank sheet and achieved the same offensive output, saving everybody the trouble of pretending there was a contest.

Every Raiders starter finished on zero. No star, no honorable mention, not even a modest contribution worth pretending to celebrate. Detroit scored eighty-four against an opponent that provided the same resistance as a disconnected controller. A manager cannot fix this with a more dramatic headline; the roster must first discover how scoring works.
Seven starters and seven zeros. The Fleeced! alarm belongs to the entire Raiders roster, not a player whose breakout is supposedly just around the corner.
Crowd mood: -24.0 (Sports-Radio Grumbling).

Vegas supporters in this fictional edition have brought pitchforks, torches and an invoice for the electricity it took to display a zero. Even that theatrical uprising is a joke about the scoreboard, not a claim that an actual riot occurred.
Minus twenty-four for an entire lineup that scored nothing is almost admirably civil. A harsher rating would be justified, but the measured mood is restlessness rather than an invented riot.

Raiders supporters have no individual villain to blame. They have an institution that submitted seven empty slots and called it a game. The next credible step is basic competence, which is a devastatingly low ambition for anybody attempting to sell a competitive franchise.

Isaiah Williams scored 15.3 while Bo Melton managed 0.0 in the same starting spot — a 15.3-point miss. Even with Isaiah Williams's extra 15.3, Las Vegas Raiders would still lose by 68.7. The substitution would not have rescued a team whose starters totaled zero. Seven starting positions, seven zeros. The manager has a roster-wide emergency and an unusually short list of innocent bystanders.

San Francisco beat Pittsburgh by 33.1. Chase Brown led at 20.1 while the Steelers produced two zeroes at running back.
The 49ers did not need an elaborate tactical masterpiece; they needed the opposing manager to submit approximately the lineup that appeared.

Chase Brown (20.1 pts) and Ashton Jeanty (18.6 pts) were productive, and Pittsburgh's two zero-point running backs did the 49ers a considerable favor. San Francisco still earned the win, but a blowout against an opponent missing an entire functional backfield is not a reason to start measuring the trophy cabinet.
Crowd mood: 13.0 (Cautious Belief).

San Francisco's imaginary fans have a champagne parade behind a float labeled 'THANK YOU, PITTSBURGH BACKFIELD.' Plus thirteen reflects a real win without pretending the opponent made it especially difficult.

Plus thirteen indicates measured optimism after a convincing win. Given the opponents' two zero-point running backs, supporters are right to enjoy the result without demanding a championship ring from the league office.

The manager can take credit for taking advantage of a bad opponent. The fans' longer-term question is whether this lineup can impose itself when the other team doesn't arrive already gift-wrapped. Approval today is not a lifetime exemption from scrutiny.

Carnell Tate scored 21.5 while Tyler Warren managed 9.1 in the same starting spot — a 12.4-point miss. The win would have grown by 12.4. The manager can enjoy the result and still explain why Tyler Warren started ahead of Carnell Tate.
The 49ers did their job. The manager should not mistake the opponent's absent production for evidence that every choice was inspired.
A convincing win deserves praise. The hot seat is for real problems, not a reporter desperate to fill space.
Brown led a win that was never seriously threatened once Pittsburgh's backfield disappeared.
Next opponent: Los Angeles Rams.

Pittsburgh brought two empty running-back slots to the party. San Francisco shouldn't plan on receiving that kind of hospitality again; winning with less help from the opposition is the next real objective.

Seattle put up 105.0 while Cleveland crawled to 53.7. Zay Flowers supplied 25.8 and the margin ballooned to 51.3.
This is not a close game ruined by bad luck. It is the sort of result that causes a manager to discover the mute button on a group chat.

Zay Flowers (25.8 pts) and Malik Nabers (23.2 pts) gave Seattle a genuine one-two punch, while Cleveland spent most of the afternoon proving it wasn't prepared to respond. Seattle earned 105 points and an easy victory. That's real production; the only ridiculous part would be treating this particular Browns performance as the league's toughest possible test.
Crowd mood: 1.0 (Jury Still Out).

Seattle's fictional victory party has fireworks, champagne and a fifty-one-point banner so large it blocks the view of Cleveland's score. Plus one says even delighted supporters can recognize an opponent that barely resisted.
Plus one after winning by more than fifty is an extraordinary endorsement of healthy skepticism. Fans have apparently noticed that Cleveland's performance supplied much of the comedy.

Keon Coleman scored 23.6 while Kyle Pitts managed 7.7 in the same starting spot — a 15.9-point miss. The win would have grown by 15.9. The manager can enjoy the result and still explain why Kyle Pitts started ahead of Keon Coleman.
Seattle's management can take credit for getting points on the board. The Browns supplied enough incompetence that excessive swagger would look silly.
There is no reason to invent a Seattle scandal in a fifty-one-point victory. The next opponent might provide legitimate questions.
Flowers did his job in a performance the scoreboard made impossible to ignore.
Next opponent: Arizona Cardinals.
Cleveland offered minimal resistance. Seattle's next job is to preserve the parts that worked against a team that doesn't fold the second it sees Zay Flowers.
